transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m constantly in motion, even when there’s no real reason to be. I’m 70, so you’d think a quiet day would be a quiet day, but I don’t really seem to do quiet very well.

Like yesterday, for instance, I had the garden club list out because I was trying to make sure I hadn’t forgotten anyone, and then I noticed my knitting bag sitting there, so I started fussing with that, and then somehow I was going through travel papers—just little things, nothing urgent—and before I knew it I hadn’t actually finished any of them. It’s like I’m bouncing from one thing to another all day long. Not in a dramatic way, maybe, but enough that it wears on me.
When you notice yourself moving from task to task like that, do you also feel worried or nervous inside, or does it feel more like you're unusually energetic and in a great mood?

I’m not sure I’d call it worried, exactly, and I don’t think it feels like I’m in some wonderful mood either. It’s more… I just sort of notice something and then I’m off doing that, and then something else catches my eye. Sometimes I’m a little keyed up, I suppose, but not necessarily nervous in the way I’d be if something bad were happening.

And it’s not like I’m cheerful and full of grand ideas or anything like that. I might be perfectly ordinary in my mood, just making tea or looking for a piece of paper, and then suddenly I’ve got three things half-done. So I don’t know which box that fits in. It just feels like my mind and my hands don’t stay in one place very long.
Has this tendency to jump between tasks and have trouble focusing been something you've noticed your whole life, or is this a new pattern that's developed recently?

Oh, no, it’s not new. I mean, I notice it more now, maybe because I have quieter days and fewer outside routines keeping me on track, but when I think back, it’s been there a very long time.

Even in grade school, my teachers would tell my mother that I was bright, but scattered. That was the word they used a lot, I think—scattered. I was forever losing papers or not having the right thing in my desk when I needed it. And I’d talk before I was supposed to, answer out of turn, that sort of thing. I remember being told to sit still because I’d wiggle around in my seat, and I’d be halfway through my work and already fiddling with something else or looking around the room.

So, no, I wouldn’t say this just suddenly came on recently. It feels more like an old pattern that’s followed me along, though I suppose it shows up differently now than it did when I was a little girl in school.

latest_inference.note: Patient describes a lifelong pattern dating back to grade school (scattered, impulsive, fidgety, distractible, blurting answers) rather than an episodic or newly acquired change, which strongly supports ADHD persisting into adulthood. This rules out F31.9 (no mood elevation/euphoria reported), F06.7 (implies an acquired organic cognitive disorder, inconsistent with lifelong childhood-onset symptoms), and E05.9 (hyperthyroidism would be a new/acquired change, not a lifelong trait).

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong (childhood-onset) pattern of distractibility, disorganization, difficulty sustaining attention on tasks, impulsive talking/answering out of turn, and motor restlessness/fidgeting. Symptoms are present across multiple settings (school, home) and persist into late adulthood, causing functional inefficiency (unfinished tasks). Mood is described as neutral/ordinary, ruling out mania/hypomania, and the restlessness is not accompanied by anxious worry, making GAD less likely. The chronic, early-onset, cross-situational inattentive-hyperactive pattern best fits ADHD, combined presentation (F90.0), persisting into adulthood.
